title: How the MPAA Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how the MPAA (Motion Picture Association of America) works, covering its origins in 1922 under Will Hayes and the Hays Code, the 1968 rating system created by Jack Valenti after the Ginzburg Supreme Court case, the current G, PG, PG-13, R, and NC-17 ratings, the secretive Classification and Rating Administration (CARA) and its raters, the submission fee, the appeals process, the MPAA's lobbying against piracy and VCRs, criticism of uneven treatment of sex, violence, and LGBT content, and the new "check the box" descriptors. Includes a listener mail segment about wild parrots in San Francisco and a recommendation of the documentary This Film Is Not Yet Rated.
topics: This Film Is Not Yet Rated

segments.title: Opening banter and framing the MPAA topic
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, note Chuck is off today, and frame the episode around the MPAA after the documentary This Film Is Not Yet Rated. Josh says rating content is valuable for parents but that the MPAA handles it poorly.
topics: This Film Is Not Yet Rated

segments.title: Origin of PG-13
segments.summary: Chuck explains PG-13 was created after Steven Spielberg's PG-rated films Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and Gremlins drew complaints, leading him to ask the MPAA for an in-between rating. PG-13 is now a commercially dominant rating, and filmmakers have added violence to PG-13 films.
topics: Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom

segments.title: The Hays Code and early Hollywood self-regulation
segments.summary: The MPAA was founded in 1922 under Will Hays, who installed the Hays Code to stop local municipalities from passing obscenity bans that hurt business. The code required morality, good triumphing over evil, and repressed sexuality.

segments.title: Decline of the Hays Code and the 1968 rating system
segments.summary: After World War Two attitudes loosened and the Hays Code faded by the late 1950s. After the Ginzburg Supreme Court case, which held that obscenity law was local, Jack Valenti created the MPAA's rating system in 1968 to avoid local censorship.

segments.title: Early X rating and history
segments.summary: The original ratings ran G through X. X was a marketing tool rather than a formal rating, and the hosts mention a Brain Stuff blog post by Christian about former X-rated movies.

segments.title: Explanation of current ratings G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17
segments.summary: The hosts go through the current ratings: G for general audiences, PG with possible violence but less tolerance for language and sex, PG-13, R with an under-17 admission suggestion, and NC-17 which replaced X in 1990 and is adult-only. The first NC-17 film was Henry & June. These are suggestions rather than laws, and theaters set their own policies.

segments.title: Voluntary submission, fees, and the CARA raters
segments.summary: Submission is nominally voluntary but in practice required for theater release, and fees range from about $25,000 for big-budget films to $750 for shorts. The Classification and Rating Administration uses raters, who are anonymous, often lack children in the stated age range, and whose process is secret. Raters vote, and a senior rater presents the rating to the filmmaker, who can accept, edit, or reject it.

segments.title: Secrecy, accountability, and the appeals process
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the secrecy of raters and the rating process draws criticism, and that Kirby Dick's documentary tailed raters and found they did not meet stated requirements. Appeals were once conducted in secret, could not reference other films, and included industry members; this changed after the documentary.

segments.title: Lobbying, conflicts of interest, and transparency calls
segments.summary: The MPAA is the lobbying arm of six major studios that take most ticket revenue. Critics say it represents those studios' interests and rates rival or foreign films more strictly. Filmmakers are asking for transparency rather than an end to ratings.

segments.title: Piracy, digital distribution, and anti-piracy laws
segments.summary: Digital distribution threatens the MPAA's power because its influence rests on ratings needed for theaters. The MPAA lobbied for the Digital Millennium Copyright Act in 2000, which made peer-to-peer movie sharing a federal crime. The hosts discuss camcorder recordings, screener leaks, watermarked copies, public screening licenses, and HBO Go piracy.

segments.title: Check the Box descriptors and marketing to kids
segments.summary: The MPAA added Check the Box descriptions explaining the reasons for a rating. Critics say these are disingenuous advertisements, and that PG-13 and R films are marketed to younger audiences through tie-ins and ads on sites popular with teens.

segments.title: Filmmakers gaming ratings and uneven treatment of content
segments.summary: Filmmakers sometimes shoot outrageous footage to trade away for a lower rating. Critics say the MPAA tolerates violence while penalizing profanity and sexuality, especially female sexual pleasure and gay relationships. Josh cites Filumena, cut to PG-13 after profanity removal.

segments.title: Inconsistent ratings examples
segments.summary: The hosts cite AV Club examples: Hostel and a gentle Irish musical Once both got R ratings in 2007, and Rushmore got R for a Playboy scene seen by children. Todd Solondz's Happiness was released unrated after NC-17 was offered. Longtime Companion got NC-17 despite no explicit sex. Afternoon Delight was cut to an R. Blue Is the Warmest Color was rated NC-17 and some theaters let teens see it.

segments.title: MPAA defense, school shootings, and recommended reading
segments.summary: The MPAA says ratings reflect how graphic content is. The hosts criticize its focus on sex over violence and cite John Oliver and an Onion article comparing school shootings to airport security. They recommend reading Kirby Dick's Rated R for Ridiculous and This Film Is Not Yet Rated.
